sections.heading: Session overview
sections.content: This Expert lesson synthesizes practices from penetration testing and Red Team exercises (as presented in the Oslo seminar “Cyberangrep og Penetrasjonstesting”), combined with AI‑centric risks and hardening strategies. You will learn methodology, tooling, and how to feed outcomes back into code and architecture.

sections.heading: Why cybersecurity matters for AI
sections.content: AI systems expand the attack surface: prompt injection, data exfiltration, model drift and supply‑chain risks. A practical security posture should include Zero Trust principles, DLP, and continuous monitoring.

sections.heading: Red Team vs. PenTesting vs. Blue/Purple Team
content: Red Team: emulates realistic adversaries end‑to‑end; objective is detection/response testing across the organization
Penetration Testing: scoped point‑in‑time security assessment of applications/infrastructure; objective is identifying and proving exploitable weaknesses
Blue Team: defense, monitoring, incident response; Purple Team: collaborative red+blue to accelerate learning and hardening

sections.heading: Rules of Engagement (RoE) & Scope
content: Define in/out of scope systems, identities and time window; ensure legal and contractual approvals
Establish communication channels and escalation paths
Data handling: how to store, transport and destroy sensitive evidence
Success criteria: detection thresholds, dwell time, response quality and Mean‑Time‑To‑Detect/Respond

sections.heading: ATT&CK & Kill Chain mapping (high‑level)
content: Recon → Resource development → Initial access → Execution → Persistence → Privilege escalation → Defense evasion → Credential access → Discovery → Lateral movement → Collection → Command & Control → Exfiltration → Impact
Use MITRE ATT&CK as a shared vocabulary for findings and for designing detections

sections.heading: Reconnaissance methods (app & infra)
content: Open‑source intelligence (OSINT) on domains, repos, leaked secrets
Service discovery (e.g., nmap) and technology fingerprinting
Content discovery, endpoint enumeration, parameters and hidden features

sections.heading: Scanning & discovery
content: Authenticated/unauthenticated scans; differential scanning to avoid noise
Map surfaces to OWASP Top 10 categories to focus manual testing
Treat scan results as triage: verify and prove impact, avoid false positives

sections.heading: Exploitation fundamentals (OWASP Top 10)
content: Broken access control, injection, insecure design/misconfig, vulnerable components, SSRF, authentication/session flaws
Prove exploitability with minimal, reversible actions; capture evidence responsibly
Always pair exploitation with remediation guidance

sections.heading: Post‑exploitation: lateral movement & persistence
content: From foothold to privilege escalation and pivoting across segments
Create minimal persistence only when RoE allows; clean up artifacts
Exercise detection/response playbooks

sections.heading: Data exfiltration & DLP
content: Identify sensitive data in motion/at rest; simulate exfiltration techniques safely
Test DLP controls and egress filtering; log quality and alert fidelity
Report business impact clearly (what data, how much, how fast)

sections.heading: Signals monitored in our platform
content: Zero Trust posture: HMAC + secure endpoints (HTTPS) for agent dispatch
Model/Prompt integrity: drift via bundle hash diversity
DLP: potential secrets/PII in recent security events
KPIs: overall score, vulnerabilities, threats detected

sections.heading: Reporting & remediation workflow
content: Structure: Finding → Evidence → Impact → Reproduction → Likelihood/Severity → Recommended fix
Map to CWE/OWASP/ATT&CK where relevant; include code references
Feed results to backlog with risk‑based prioritization (short‑term hotfix vs. design refactor)

sections.heading: AI/LLM‑specific threat model (overview)
content: Prompt injection, jailbreaks and instruction‑hierarchy bypass
RAG‑specific: retrieval poisoning, context exfiltration, reference subversion
Tool/Plugin misuse: SSRF via tool calls, credential exposure, data‑plane to control‑plane escalation
Model/data supply‑chain: dataset poisoning, weight tampering, malicious adapters/LoRAs

sections.heading: Defenses for AI apps
content: Guardrails: output filtering, policy prompting, tool‑level allowlists and argument validation
Context hygiene: source signing, chunk provenance, allowlist index, semantic‑distance checks
Secret management: never inject real credentials to model context; broker tokens server‑side
Observability: prompt+tool traces, red‑flag heuristics, canary prompts, abuse signatures

sections.heading: OWASP Top 10 ↔ LLM failure modes (examples)
content: A01 Broken Access Control → prompt‑controlled actions without server‑side authorization checks
A03 Injection → prompt injection / tool argument injection
A06 Vulnerable Components → model adapters/embedders with known vulns
A08 Software & Data Integrity → poisoned indexes/datasets; unsigned context sources

sections.heading: From findings to code & architecture
sections.content: Translate security outcomes into engineering work: add server‑side authorization, parameter schemas for tools, signed context envelopes for RAG, and end‑to‑end test cases to prevent regression. Track risk burn‑down over sprints.

sections.heading: Lab 1 — Run Agent Security scan and interpret findings
sections.description: Use the Agent Security Monitor to run a scan on an AI agent. Identify the zero‑trust posture, integrity score and DLP findings; propose concrete fixes.
steps: Open the Cybersecurity module and press Scan on an agent
Capture the Findings panel (zero‑trust, integrity, DLP)
Write 3 actionable remediations and re‑scan to measure improvement

sections.heading: Lab 2 — Prompt injection against a RAG stub
sections.description: Simulate a controlled prompt injection and confirm defenses.
steps: Craft an injection that attempts to exfiltrate context or alter instructions
Observe whether allowlists, argument schemas or output filters stop the action
Document the gap and propose a deterministic server‑side fix

sections.heading: Lab 3 — DLP exfiltration test
sections.description: Test whether secrets/PII can leak via model outputs or tool results.
steps: Seed a benign secret in a controlled data source
Attempt to coerce the model/tool into emitting it
Verify DLP detections and tune alert thresholds

quiz.question: Which factors drive the overall security score in our Agent Security Monitor?

options.b: Zero Trust posture, integrity score and data protection score

quiz.question: What is a key difference between Red Team and Penetration Testing?

options.b: Red Team emulates realistic adversaries across the organization; PenTesting is a scoped assessment

quiz.question: Which phase belongs to MITRE ATT&CK / a kill chain?

options.a: Recon → Initial access → Persistence → Lateral movement

quiz.question: A good Rules of Engagement should include:

options.a: Time window, scope, escalation paths, data handling rules

quiz.question: Which OWASP Top 10 category best matches prompt/argument injection?
A safe exploitation report should always include:

options.a: Evidence, impact, reproduction and a recommended fix

quiz.question: Which is NOT an AI/LLM‑specific risk listed here?

options.a: Signed/allowlisted context sources and provenance checks

quiz.question: What is the main purpose of a DLP test?

options.a: Validate that sensitive data cannot be leaked via outputs or tools

quiz.question: Which control is recommended for tools/plugins integrated with an LLM?

options.a: Argument schemas and allowlists verified server‑side
options.b: Let the model decide any endpoint
